how-much-to-charge-for-a-broken-spring.h.text:
← Garage door bid calculator

How much to charge for a broken garage door spring

The call is almost always “the door won’t open.” The job is almost always a torsion spring. The price that gets advertised — $189, $249, “we beat any quote” — treats the kit and an hour in the driveway as the whole cost. The van still had to get there.

Work a weekday spring ticket

Kit on a 16×7: roughly $175 from a supplier, more for high-cycle. Shop time: about an hour and a quarter if the tracks and cables are honest. Loaded wage (wage plus burden) on a $28 tech at 30% burden is $36.40. That is about $45 of shop labor. Then the drive: forty minutes each way is 40 miles at 30 mph — $32 of vehicle cost at $0.80/mile plus $48 of travel labor. The ticket already costs about $300 before overhead. A $189 special is underwater by more than a hundred dollars.

The same ticket eight miles from the shop can still clear a 25% margin. Distance is the product, not the spring.

After-hours is not a favor

Evening and weekend premiums belong on shop labor. They do not make the miles cheaper. If you only raise the advertised special by $40 and drive across town at 8 p.m., you paid for the privilege.

Price it before you roll

The garage door bid calculator flags a spring job when travel is 35% or more of the price, or when the drive costs more than the hour in the driveway. Use it to decide whether to quote a trip fee, raise the ticket, or pass. It is not a safety inspection and it does not tell you the door is safe to operate.

Common questions

How much should I charge for a broken garage door spring?

Charge the spring kit, the shop hour at a loaded wage, travel labor plus miles, then overhead and margin. A advertised $189 special is often below cost once the van has driven forty minutes each way.

Should I replace the door instead of the spring?

Only if the door itself is the problem. A rusted, uninsulated slab may need replacement, but quoting a full door when the customer called for a spring is how the job walks to the next truck. Price both tickets and let the customer choose.

No warranty. This is not legal, tax, financial, engineering, or business advice, and it does not tell you what to charge. Springs are dangerous; follow the manufacturer procedure and your training. The authors accept no liability for loss or damage from its use.

how-much-to-charge-to-replace-a-garage-d.text:
← Garage door bid calculator

How much to charge to replace a garage door

Homeowners type that question and get a $800–$3,500 range. A shop that copies the middle of that range loses money on the far jobs and leaves money on the close ones. Charge the ticket you can actually deliver: parts + loaded shop hours + the drive + overhead + the margin you intend to keep.

The lines that belong on the bid

  1. The slab. Square footage × what your supplier invoices for that construction (non-insulated steel, R-9, R-16, wood, aluminum/glass). Decorative windows and wind-load hardware are extras, not included in the slab line.
  2. The spring kit. A double torsion pack is not two singles. High-cycle springs cost more and belong on high-use doors.
  3. The opener, if it is on this ticket. Chain, belt, or jackshaft. Battery backup and wifi are adders. A replacement that reuses a working opener should not carry a new-unit cost.
  4. Shop hours. Time on site, timed from your own crew. Starting points in the calculator are ballpark only.
  5. Travel. Round-trip miles × vehicle cost, plus drive hours × loaded wage. This is the line a neighborhood lump sum hides.
  6. Overhead and margin of price — not a markup on cost, because that is how the customer’s number and your P&L read.

Why a 16×7 is not two 8×7s

The door area is double, so the slab is about double. The trip is one trip. The opener is one opener. Setup, safety-reverse, and the second tech standing there do not double. Shops that quote “two singles” overprice the double and still underprice the drive on a far single.

Use the calculator

The garage door bid calculator runs the arithmetic in your browser. Nothing is uploaded. Replace every starting figure with your invoice and a timed job before you send the number.

Common questions

How much should I charge to replace a garage door?

Price parts (slab, springs, hardware, disposal), shop labor at a loaded wage, travel labor plus vehicle miles, then overhead and a margin of price. A typical insulated 16×7 with a new belt-drive opener is not twice a single 8×7 because travel and the opener happen once.

Is a double door twice a single?

No. The slab is about twice the square footage, but the trip, the opener, and much of the setup happen once. Labor on a 16×7 replacement is closer to 1.3× an 8×7 than 2×.

No warranty. This is not legal, tax, financial, engineering, or business advice, and it does not tell you what to charge. Verify outputs against your own costs and a qualified professional. The authors accept no liability for loss or damage from its use.

FOR GARAGE DOOR TECHS AND SMALL SHOPS

Bid the spring, the door, and the drive — not a lump sum.

Price a replacement or a broken-spring service the way the ticket actually costs: parts, shop hours, and the miles to get there. A 16×7 is not two 8×7s, and a $189 spring special forty minutes each way is often a loss before the hood goes up.

How much to charge to replace a garage door · How much to charge for a broken spring · vs. Housecall Pro · vs. a flat $189 broken-spring special

The ticket

Pick the job and the opening. Suggested parts and hours fill in as a starting point and stay put once you edit them — your supplier invoice beats our ballpark.

Parts

High-cycle springs, wind-load hardware, and decorative windows belong in hardware or the spring line — they are not free upgrades on a replacement that already looked tight.

Labor, travel, and margin

After-hours multiplies shop labor only. Travel still costs the loaded wage for the drive plus the miles — evenings do not make the van cheaper.

Hand the customer a proposal

The price above is for you. This is the page you print or save as a PDF and give to the customer — your details, their details, the scope, the deposit split, and a line for them to sign. Your business details are saved on this device so you only type them once; the customer’s details are never saved.

Everything on the printed page is text you typed or a number this calculator worked out. It contains no warranty, lien, or cancellation wording — those depend on your jurisdiction and your contract, and this tool is not the place to invent them.

Where the price goes

    Transparent arithmetic from your own inputs. The starting part and hour figures are common ballpark numbers, not a manufacturer list, a code requirement, or a guarantee — replace them with your supplier invoice and a timed job.

    Common questions

    What does this garage door estimate include?

    The ticket price adds up parts — door/slab, spring kit, opener unit, hardware, disposal, and permit — plus shop labor on site, travel (both the drive-time labor and vehicle cost per mile), overhead, and your target margin. Job type decides which parts lines actually apply: a spring-only ticket zeroes out the door and opener cost unless you enter one anyway.

    Why does travel get its own line instead of being folded into overhead?

    A short shop job forty minutes each way is a different ticket from the same job around the corner, and a flat overhead percentage hides that. Travel is priced as loaded wage for the drive time plus a per-mile vehicle cost, and the tool flags “travel eats job” when travel is at least 35% of a spring-only ticket, or exceeds shop labor on any job — the exact trap a $189 special forty minutes out falls into.

    Why is a double door not just two single doors?

    Job type sets separate suggested labor hours for single versus double openings (the split is at 10 ft of width), because a double door’s extra track, larger panel, and heavier spring kit take more shop time per opening than doubling a single-door job would suggest — suggested hours, spring cost, and door cost all key off which class the width falls into.

    Why do suggested parts and hours change when I pick a different job type or door?

    Changing job type, door size, construction, or opener re-applies each preset's suggested figure to every field you haven't hand-edited yet — so switching from “door + new opener” to “broken-spring service” zeroes the door and opener cost automatically. Once you edit a field yourself, later preset changes leave it alone.

    Is my data uploaded anywhere?

    No account and no network requests — the calculator runs entirely in your browser. This calculator does not save your ticket inputs between visits, but a share link encodes only the inputs you choose into the address bar and is never sent to us; only your business name and contact details for the printed proposal are kept in this browser's local storage, and “Forget my business details” clears them.

    Does this cover wind load, permits, or spring safety?

    No. Hours and part costs are ballpark shop figures you can edit, not a building-code or engineering determination, a wind-load calculation, or a permit approval. High-cycle springs and wind-load hardware are cost lines you choose to add, not something the tool checks your opening needs — and spring and opener work carries real injury risk that belongs to a qualified installer, not this arithmetic.

    No warranty. This free tool is not legal, tax, financial, engineering, or business advice, and it does not tell you what to charge. It is not a safety inspection, a wind-load calculation, or a permit determination. Verify every figure against your own payroll, insurance, supplier invoices, and a qualified professional before relying on it or submitting a bid. vs-a-flat-189-broken-spring-special.html.text:
← Garage Door Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat $189 broken-spring special

Broken-spring service is advertised as one flat number — $189, $249, "we beat any quote." That rate cannot see door class, spring cycle, or the drive, and the same special that clears a small profit six miles from the shop loses money outright forty minutes away.

What a flat broken-spring special is

It is the fastest number to put on a postcard or a search ad: one price, no questions asked, whatever the door turns out to be when the tech arrives. It is learned on a job that was easy to price — usually a single door, a standard-cycle spring, and a short drive — and then quoted again on the next call that comes in.

Nothing about the phone call tells the shop whether the next door is a single or a double, whether the spring is standard or high-cycle, or how far the van has to drive. The special does not ask, because it was never built to answer.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter the job type, door width and height, spring kit cost, shop hours, and round-trip miles, plus your own wage, payroll burden, vehicle cost per mile, overhead, and target margin. It prices the ticket from what this specific door and this specific drive actually cost, not a number learned on the last call.

What a flat $189 special doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same rate for a single 8×7 door and a double 16×7 door, even though the double takes a heavier spring kit and more shop minutes. Prices the spring kit and shop hours from the door's own class (single or double), so a double door costs more without anyone eyeballing a surcharge.
Has no line for spring cycle — a standard-cycle kit and a high-cycle kit, which this calculator's own defaults price 1.6x apart, get the same rate. Prices a high-cycle spring kit at its own higher parts cost, entered directly rather than guessed.
Has no line for travel — a 6-mile round trip and a 42-mile round trip get the same rate. Prices drive time and vehicle miles separately, and reports the travel share of the price so a short hop and a long haul are never quoted the same.
Gives the tech a number to quote over the phone, not a number to check a quote against. Flags the ticket when travel eats the job — when travel cost is at least 35% of a spring-only ticket's price, or exceeds the shop labor cost outright.
Cannot tell you when $189 is a loss rather than a thin margin. Reports the break-even cost and the price at your target margin, so a flat special can be scored against real cost before you match it.

Same special, two different tickets

Using this calculator's own shipped cost inputs — $28 hourly wage, 30% payroll burden, $0.75 a mile, 15% overhead, 25% target margin:

A nearby single 8×7 door with a standard-cycle spring kit and a 6-mile round trip (0.2 drive hours) costs $164.66 to run, with travel at $11.78 — 5.4% of the price — and this calculator prices the ticket at $219.54. A flat $189 special still clears $24.34 here, a 12.9% margin, below the 25% target but not a loss.

The same $189 special quoted on a distant double 16×7 door with a high-cycle spring kit and a 42-mile round trip (1.4 drive hours) is a different story. That ticket costs $469.15 to run — travel alone is $82.46, 13.2% of the price and more than the $45.50 of shop labor, which is exactly what trips this calculator's own travel-eats-the-job flag. This calculator prices the ticket at $625.54. The flat $189 special is $280.15 below the job's own break-even cost — a loss, not a thin margin — and $436.54 below what this calculator would charge at a 25% margin. Same advertised number, one ticket profitable and one underwater, and nothing about the phone call that took the booking told the shop which one was coming.

Common questions

Why does a flat $189 broken-spring special get a bid wrong?

Because the number is learned on one job -- typically a nearby single door with a standard-cycle spring -- and then quoted sight unseen on the next call, whatever the door class, spring cycle, or drive turns out to be. This calculator's own shipped defaults price a nearby single-door standard-spring ticket at $219.54 against a total cost of $164.66, so a $189 special still clears $24.34 there. The same $189 special quoted on a distant double door with a high-cycle spring is $280.15 below that job's $469.15 break-even cost -- a loss, not a thin margin, on a job this calculator prices at $625.54.

What does a flat broken-spring special usually miss entirely?

Door class (a double door takes a heavier torsion kit and more shop minutes than a single), spring cycle (a high-cycle kit runs 1.6x a standard kit's cost), and travel (drive time and vehicle miles do not shrink because the ticket is a spring, not a door). A flat rate has no line for any of them -- it is one number learned on one job and reused for the next call that comes in, regardless of how far the van has to go.

How big is the pricing gap in practice?

Using this calculator's own shipped cost inputs -- $28 hourly wage, 30% burden, $0.75 a mile, 15% overhead, 25% target margin: a nearby single 8x7 door with a standard-cycle spring and a 6-mile round trip costs $164.66 to run and this calculator prices it at $219.54. A distant double 16x7 door with a high-cycle spring and a 42-mile round trip costs $469.15 to run and prices at $625.54. Quoting both at the same $189 flat special leaves $24.34 on the near job and a $280.15 loss on the far one -- a swing of over $500 hidden inside one advertised number.

Is a flat broken-spring special ever a reasonable shorthand?

For calls that stay close to the shop, on single doors with a standard-cycle spring, a flat number can land close to cost. The risk is quoting a double door, a high-cycle kit, or a long drive the same way over the phone, because the advertised rate does not know any of that until the tech is already on site -- and by then the $189 has often already been promised.

Does this calculator know my local labor rates or parts pricing?

No. It has no data on your local labor market or your supplier's kit pricing. It takes the job type, door size, spring kit, shop hours, and round-trip miles, plus your own wage, payroll burden, vehicle cost per mile, overhead, and target margin, and turns that into a price for this ticket -- the arithmetic a flat special skips, not a market survey.

vs-housecall-pro.html.text:
← Garage Door Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. Housecall Pro

Two different shapes: Housecall Pro is an account-based platform for running a garage-door (or HVAC, plumbing, electrical) company's whole operation, including scheduling and invoicing a job once it is priced. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — what should this door or spring ticket cost, before you offer it to the customer.

What each tool is for

Housecall Pro is a field-service management platform marketed to garage door, HVAC, plumbing, electrical and other home-service businesses. It is used to run CRM and customer records, scheduling and dispatch, online booking, invoicing and payments, and a mobile app for technicians in the field, tied to one account used on an ongoing basis across every job the company runs. Housecall Pro's own site is not reachable from this session to confirm today's specific feature list, plan names, or pricing, so only its well-documented identity and category are stated here: nothing about it is invented, and no dollar figure for it appears on this page. Public descriptions of that scheduling and invoicing software describe running and billing a job once its scope and price already exist; none describe working out what a new garage-door ticket should cost from door size, parts, shop hours and drive time before you quote it — which is the one thing this calculator does.

This calculator does none of what Housecall Pro does. It does not store a customer record, dispatch a technician, or invoice anyone. It takes one ticket — job type, door size and construction, parts (door, spring kit, opener, hardware, disposal, permit), shop labor hours, and round-trip travel — and turns that into the ticket price, the price per square foot of door, the effective hourly rate, and the walk-away price below which the job loses money — plus, if you already have a number on the table, a check of whether it clears your own break-even floor, and a printable customer proposal. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.

I need to store customer records, dispatch techs, and invoice customers for door jobs across my whole business.Housecall Pro, or a comparable field-service platform — running that ongoing operation is not something this calculator does.

Is a cheap spring special still worth it forty minutes each way?This calculator flags “travel eats job” when the drive is eating the ticket, before you dispatch anyone.
A customer's budget is below what I'd normally quote. Does it still clear my walk-away floor?This calculator's proposed-price check — it flags a price below break-even before you agree to it.
I already have jobs priced and need to schedule, invoice and track them across many customers and technicians.Housecall Pro — built as an ongoing, account-based platform for exactly that job.
How does the math behind a door or spring ticket actually work?This calculator's own door-replacement walkthrough and broken-spring walkthrough.
Do I need to create an account or sign up to use the tool?This calculator: no. Housecall Pro's tools are used through a paid account.

Most garage-door businesses get different value from each: Housecall Pro (or a comparable field-service platform) for running customers, scheduling and invoicing across an ongoing business as an account, and a private calculator like this one for an instant, no-login answer to what a new door or spring ticket should cost before it is offered. This page's own figures are a pricing model, not a signed proposal or an invoice.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or Housecall Pro?

They do different jobs, and a garage-door business of any size will likely end up touching both. Housecall Pro is a field-service management platform marketed to garage door, HVAC, plumbing, electrical and other home-service companies, used to run CRM and customer records, scheduling and dispatch, invoicing and online payments, and a technician mobile app across a whole operation, on an ongoing paid account. This calculator does one narrower thing: it takes a single ticket's job type, door size and construction, parts (door, spring kit, opener, hardware, disposal, permit), shop labor, and round-trip travel, and turns that into the ticket price, the price per square foot of door, the effective hourly rate, and the walk-away price below which the job loses money, before you have quoted anything. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type. A company already scheduling routes and invoicing customers across many jobs is better served by Housecall Pro or a comparable field-service platform; a tech who needs an instant, private answer to what one door or spring ticket should cost before it is offered is in the right place here.
